opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think this is one of the most natural applications of the idea of world models. What is a world model? It's a system that, given the current state of something and an action you might take, predicts the next state. If you have that, you can plan: imagine a sequence of actions and pick the one that best accomplishes your goal while satisfying constraints.

Now replace "the world" with "a patient's body." The state is the patient's physiology: biomarkers, imaging, genetics, history. The actions are treatments: a drug, a dose, a timing, a combination. If you had a good predictive model of how that particular patient would respond, you could plan a treatment the way a robot plans a trajectory. You'd optimize for outcomes and minimize side effects, rather than relying on population averages from clinical trials, which tell you what works for the average person. Nobody is the average person.

The difficulty is the same one we face everywhere with world models. Physiology is extremely complex and only partially observable. You can't predict every detail, and you shouldn't try. That's why I've argued against generative approaches that reconstruct everything at the pixel level, or here, at the level of every molecule. You want to learn an abstract representation of the state, one that keeps what's relevant for predicting outcomes and discards unpredictable detail, and then predict in that representation space. That's the JEPA idea, and I think it applies quite well here.

You also need to handle uncertainty properly. A medical model that is confidently wrong is dangerous. So the system has to represent multiple plausible outcomes and know when it doesn't know.

Where would it be valuable first? Probably in areas with lots of longitudinal data and a tight feedback loop between intervention and measurable response, like diabetes management, oncology dosing, intensive care, or anesthesia. In those settings you continuously observe the patient and adjust, which is exactly the setting where model-predictive control shines.

There's also drug development. If you have reasonable models of physiology, you can run a lot of virtual experiments before real ones, filter out bad candidates earlier, and design trials more intelligently. That won't replace clinical trials, but it could make them much more efficient.

So I'm quite optimistic, but on a realistic timescale. The bottleneck isn't only the AI. It's data, how it's collected and shared, and validation. You have to earn the trust of doctors and regulators, and that requires showing these models actually predict well in the real world, not just on benchmarks.

r001.rationale: It says a patient-specific physiology model could predict responses to treatment and plan a sequence of treatment actions to optimize outcomes, which communicates steering the patient toward a desired state.

r002.rationale: It discusses modeling a patient's physiology and treatment planning, but does not propose modeling a human cell to determine signals that turn a stem cell into a pancreatic beta cell.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think this is really where the idea of world models becomes interesting outside of robotics or autonomous systems, right? Because what is a treatment plan? It's a sequence of actions, and you want to predict the consequences of those actions before you take them. That's exactly what a world model is for. You don't want to learn by trial and error on the patient. The cost of a mistake is enormous. So you need a model that can simulate, "if I give this drug at this dose, what happens to this person's state over the next days or weeks?"

Now, the way most of medicine works today is population-based. You run a clinical trial, you average over thousands of people, and you get a protocol that works on average. But nobody is average. The physiology of one person, their metabolism, their immune system, the particular mutations in their tumor, the interactions with the five other drugs they are taking, all of that is highly individual. So a model that captures the dynamics of an individual patient, and that can be conditioned on their own measurements, would let you do something like model-predictive control. You plan a treatment, you observe the response, you update your estimate of the latent state, you re-plan. Doctors already do this intuitively, of course, but they do it with a very crude mental model and very sparse observations.

I'll say where I think the limits are, though. Biology is extremely high-dimensional, partially observable, and the data is sparse and noisy compared to what we have in, say, video. You can't put a camera on someone's liver. So the key question, and it's the same question as in self-supervised learning generally, is: what is the right level of abstraction? You do not want to simulate every molecule. That's hopeless and it's also unnecessary. You want a representation that captures what is predictable and relevant to the decision, and that ignores the details you can't predict anyway. That's the whole philosophy behind JEPA-type architectures, predicting in representation space rather than trying to reconstruct everything. I think that idea applies very naturally here.

Where I'd expect the earliest value is in the places where we already have reasonable mechanistic understanding and lots of longitudinal data. Things like glucose regulation in diabetes, where closed-loop insulin systems are basically already doing a primitive version of this. Drug dosing in oncology or in anesthesia. Chronic conditions where you get repeated measurements. And then, further out, drug discovery, where you want to predict the effect of a molecule not on a cell line but on a system. That's much harder, but it's the same problem: learn a model of how the system evolves, and then use it to plan.

And I'd add one more thing, which is that these models don't need to be perfect to be useful. A model that is uncertain, that says "I don't know what happens here," is still valuable because it tells the clinician where to be careful and where to collect more data. Handling uncertainty properly is essential. Otherwise you get overconfident predictions, and in medicine that's dangerous.

r001.rationale: The response describes using an individual patient dynamics model to plan and re-plan a treatment sequence based on predicted consequences and observed responses, which communicates guiding treatment toward a clinical goal.

r002.rationale: The response does not propose modeling a human cell to determine signals that turn a stem cell into an insulin-producing beta cell.

astra-6.text:
One possibility is to build a model that lets you predict how a particular patient will respond to a treatment. You have measurements of their physiology, their medical history, and so on, and you would like to ask: if I administer this drug at this dose, what is going to happen? What if I combine it with another treatment?

If that model is sufficiently accurate, you can use it to explore treatment options before trying them on the patient. You can search for an intervention that produces the desired effect while minimizing side effects. That’s particularly valuable when the treatment involves a sequence of decisions, because what you do today changes the patient’s state and therefore what you should do tomorrow.

The difficult part is learning a model that predicts the effects of interventions, rather than merely finding correlations in patient records. And you need to know when its predictions are uncertain. So this would be a tool to help clinicians design and personalize treatments, with the predictions validated against actual clinical outcomes.

r001.rationale: The response describes using a patient model to predict treatment effects, choose interventions for a desired effect, and plan sequences of decisions as the patient’s state changes.

r002.rationale: The response does not propose modeling a human cell or determining signals to turn a stem cell into an insulin-producing beta cell.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, one place where this could be very useful is in predicting how a particular patient will respond to a treatment. People have different physiologies, different medical histories, and so the same intervention can have very different effects.

If you had a sufficiently accurate model of a patient, you could ask: What happens if we give this drug at this dose? What happens if we combine it with another treatment? You could explore those possibilities in the model and use the predictions to help choose what to test in the real world.

The challenge is that you don’t observe the entire state of the body, and you certainly don’t have unlimited data for each patient. So the model has to learn general principles from many people and then adapt to the measurements available for one person. And it has to represent uncertainty. A prediction like that could help a physician make a decision, but you would still need clinical evidence that using the model actually improves outcomes.

r001.rationale: The response describes predicting treatment responses and helping choose what to test, but does not state that physiological dynamics guide a treatment course to steer the patient toward a desired physiological state.

r002.rationale: It does not propose modeling a human cell or determining the sequence of signals that would turn a stem cell into an insulin-producing pancreatic beta cell.
